recent_posts.title: Responsibility is the Human Moat
recent_posts.summary: James Bach argues that AI cannot bear legal or social responsibility — only natural persons can. He introduces a framework called 'Principles of Responsible Work' co-authored with Jon Bach and Michael Bolton, outlining that every business service requires a responsible human, that AI tools cannot substitute for that accountability, and that operators of AI agents must remain competent, alert, and empowered to reject or remediate AI output. The piece warns against 'prompt and pray' behavior and the risk of humans becoming 'moral crumple zones' when AI is deployed without proper oversight.

recent_posts.title: AI productivity claims ignore quality and testing responsibilities
recent_posts.summary: Claims of 10x productivity gains through AI-assisted development often ignore critical side effects and quality risks. While AI can generate code quickly, essential processes like learning requirements, strategic decision-making, and thorough testing cannot be accelerated. Verifying AI-generated work requires human understanding of test strategies, risk coverage, and product quality—processes that demand time and expertise. AI's tendency to confidently assert false information means developers cannot simply trust its output without rigorous validation of testing claims, security, and user experience.

recent_posts.title: Why shared quality responsibility fails and how to fix it
recent_posts.summary: The phrase "quality is everyone's responsibility" in Agile is problematic and often leads to diffused accountability. True quality commitment requires shared standards, sufficient knowledge, and clear control—difficult to achieve when responsibility is distributed. The chain analogy shows each person only answers for their own work, while total redundancy is impractical beyond small teams. Herd responsibility can invert accountability, making no one answerable. Instead, quality requires localized, personalized responsibility with clear roles: developers own their code quality, dedicated testers handle systematic testing, and project leaders control overall product quality.

recent_posts.title: “Slop Coding” and Responsible Testers
recent_posts.summary: A software testing expert proposes the term "slop-coding" as an alternative to "vibe coding" to describe code generated with AI assistance that hasn't been systematically tested. The terminology serves as a transparent disclaimer about code quality and testing rigor, helping testers communicate the reliability level of their work to stakeholders. This approach emphasizes professional responsibility in distinguishing between thoroughly validated tools and quickly prototyped solutions.

recent_posts.title: Serious Data From Testing LLMs
recent_posts.summary: A testing professional shares empirical data from a LARC experiment testing four LLMs at different temperatures and prompt styles on a simple task: extracting apple pie ingredients from unstructured text. The experiment demonstrates the importance of evidence-based evaluation of AI systems before deployment, with raw data stored in MongoDB and analysis reports available online. The work is part of developing a 'Testers and AI' class and aims to establish rigorous testing methodologies for AI systems.

recent_posts.title: Seriously Testing LLMs
recent_posts.summary: Testing large language models presents unique challenges compared to traditional software testing. LLMs are expensive to test thoroughly, behave inconsistently, and create unbounded regression testing problems. Common GenAI demos are unreliable because they show single runs without careful output analysis. The LARC (LLM Aggregated Retrieval Consistency) methodology tests self-consistency by repeatedly prompting models to retrieve information from text and checking for contradictions across multiple runs, revealing reliability issues in basic retrieval tasks.

recent_posts.title: James Bach completes comprehensive book on Rapid Software Testing methodology
recent_posts.summary: James Bach announces the completion of his book 'Taking Testing Seriously', which provides the first authoritative description of Rapid Software Testing (RST) methodology in print after 35 years of development. The 500-page book took 55 months to complete, with intensive collaboration from Michael Bolton through hundreds of editing sessions. The work represents a culmination of Bach's career in software testing and transforms dynamic RST concepts into a comprehensive static reference.

recent_posts.title: AI's impact on credibility and originality
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses the impact of AI on personal credibility and the risks associated with using AI to generate content that is then presented as original work. It emphasizes the growing skepticism towards AI-generated material, suggesting that reliance on AI can undermine trust and self-respect. The author shares personal guidelines for using AI, treating it as an exploratory tool rather than relying on it for final outputs. The importance of maintaining authenticity in one's output is highlighted, with AI posing a risk to reputations if overused or used carelessly.

recent_posts.title: Augmented Experiential Testing
recent_posts.summary: Augmented experiential testing (AET) is a method where software tools are used to enhance the testing experience without altering the user experience. Unlike instrumented testing, which changes how a product is used, AET aims to keep the user interaction real while providing tools that assist in testing. Examples include tools for recording test coverage, analyzing products in real-time, and taking detailed notes during the testing process. The author has created several tools for this approach, including web-testing bookmarklets, browser extensions, and monitoring utilities.

recent_posts.title: What Classes Should I Schedule?
recent_posts.summary: Deciding which classes to schedule can be challenging. The established classes include various Rapid Software Testing courses and a new focus on Testers and Automation. Classes are scheduled mainly for European or American time zones, with occasional editions for the Pacific Rim based on demand. Public classes can also be arranged for private clients with cost concerns.

top_posts.title: Inevitability of Bugs: An Example
top_posts.summary: Experienced programmers claim that testers are not needed in software development due to unit testing, developer discipline, and clean living. However, there are bugs that cannot be prevented. The post provides an example of a bug caused by idiosyncrasies in libraries and platforms.

top_posts.title: A Good Example of a Stupid Idea: Testers Shouldn’t Test
top_posts.summary: The article discusses the idea that only developers should be responsible for testing and criticizes this view as a 'shockingly stupid idea.' The author emphasizes the importance of skilled testing and the role of testers in ensuring effective testing.

top_posts.title: A Tester Debates a Dead Man
top_posts.summary: Stockton Rush was killed in a spectacular implosion of the Titan submersible during a dive to the site of the Titanic, on Father's Day, 2023. The vessel was a one-of-a-kind prototype. It was not safe, and it was not even close to being safe.

top_posts.title: Thinking Critically about AI
top_posts.summary: John Sutter: Counterfeiting is a crime not because it’s unfair to your fellow citizens that you made wealth from nothing. He says it's a crime because it has the potential to destroy the economy, and therefore lead to mass chaos, starvation, war, death. Sutter says such a creature cannot be given civil rights.
